topics: 🚪 A Torah Scroll in the Bedroom — a cloak on a chest, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's ten-handbreadth partition, and Mar Zutra's rebuke
🚽 Praying Opposite a Bathroom — behind vs. in front, empty bathrooms, new structures and Persian toilets
💧 A Zav Who Saw Keri — the last mishna of chapter three and Rabbi Yehuda's exemption
🕰️ Chapter Four Opens — deadlines for morning, afternoon, evening and additional prayers
🔁 Making Up a Missed Prayer — 'its day passed, its sacrifice is void' versus 'prayer is mercy'
👴 Patriarchs or Offerings? — Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi on who instituted the prayers

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Chapter Three Ends, Chapter Four Begins
overview.subtitle: Berakhot 26a–26b
overview.hebrewSource: תְּפִלַּת הַשַּׁחַר עַד חֲצוֹת. רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: עַד אַרְבַּע שָׁעוֹת
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf finishes chapter three with two loose ends: how to shield a Torah scroll during marital relations (a cloak over a chest counts as a vessel within a vessel, and a ten-handbreadth partition is only for one who has no other room), and how far one distances himself from feces — four cubits behind, but out of sight in front, with a chain of challenges about empty bathrooms. A final mishna rules that a zav who experienced a seminal emission still needs immersion, while Rabbi Yehuda exempts him. Chapter four, Tefillat HaShaḥar, then opens with the mishna's deadlines for each prayer: morning until noon (Rabbi Yehuda: four hours), afternoon until evening (Rabbi Yehuda: pelag haminḥa), evening with no fixed time, and Musaf all day (Rabbi Yehuda: seven hours). The Gemara asks whether a missed prayer can be made up at the next one, distinguishes error from deliberate omission, and traces the whole system to either the Patriarchs or the Temple offerings.

slides.title: 🚽 May One Pray Opposite a Bathroom?
slides.subtitle: Rav Huna's 'out of sight in front' meets Rav Ḥisda's leniency

nodes.content: 📜 Mishna: distance four cubits from urine and feces. Rav Huna: only when they are behind him; in front, he moves until they are out of sight (מְלֹא עֵינָיו) — and the same for prayer
❓ But Rav Ḥisda said one may stand opposite a bathroom and pray!
💡 Answer: a bathroom with no feces in it
❓ But Rav Yosef bar Ḥanina said 'the bathroom the Sages spoke of' is even one with no feces, and 'the bathhouse' is even one with no one in it!

columns.label: New structure
columns.content: Rav Ḥisda means a building made as a bathroom but never yet used

columns.label: Ravina's dilemma
columns.content: Ravina asked whether designating a place as a bathroom takes effect — but only about praying inside it, not opposite it

nodes.content: ✅ Rava: Persian bathrooms, though they contain feces, are considered sealed, since the waste rolls away underground

callout.label: Closing chapter three:
callout.text: A cloak on a chest is a vessel within a vessel. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi requires a ten-handbreadth partition before a Torah scroll — but when Mar Zutra saw one in Mar bar Rav Ashi's bedroom he objected: that is for someone with no other room; you have another room! ('It did not enter my mind.') The chapter's last mishna: a zav who had a seminal emission, a menstruating woman who discharged semen, and a woman who saw menstrual blood after relations all need immersion; Rabbi Yehuda exempts — and, per Rabbi Ḥiyya, he exempts even one who had the emission first and then became a zav.

slides.title: 🕰️ Chapter Four: How Late May Each Prayer Be Said?
slides.subtitle: The mishna's deadlines and the baraita that anchors them in the Temple offerings
rows: The morning tamid may be offered until noon; Rabbi Yehuda: until four hours
The afternoon tamid is offered until evening; Rabbi Yehuda: until pelag haminḥa
Limbs and fats not consumed by evening burn on the altar all night
The Musaf offering is brought all day; Rabbi Yehuda: until seven hours

callout.label: Two minḥas:
callout.text: Minḥa gedola begins at six and a half hours, minḥa ketana at nine and a half. Rabbi Yehuda's pelag is the midpoint of the last minḥa — eleven hours less a quarter. And a baraita saying the mitzva of Shema is at sunrise so as to join redemption to prayer in daytime? That is the vatikin, who finish Shema at sunrise (Rabbi Yoḥanan).

slides.title: 🔁 Can a Missed Prayer Be Made Up?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Yoḥanan's rulings, a dilemma about minḥa, and a verse from Ecclesiastes

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: Does everyone really hold the morning prayer ends at noon? Rabbi Yoḥanan said: one who erred and skipped the evening prayer prays twice in the morning; skipped the morning — prays twice at minḥa!

lines.speaker: Answer
lines.text: One may keep praying all day. Until noon he receives the reward of prayer at its time; afterward, the reward of prayer but not of prayer at its time.

lines.speaker: Dilemma
lines.text: Skipped minḥa — may he pray twice in the evening? Evening and morning are one day, 'there was evening and there was morning, one day' (Genesis 1:5). But minḥa and ma'ariv are two days, and prayer stands in place of a sacrifice: כֵּיוָן דְּעָבַר יוֹמוֹ בָּטַל קׇרְבָּנוֹ, once its day passed, its offering is void. Or is prayer mercy, offered whenever one wishes?

lines.speaker: R' Yoḥanan
lines.text: Rav Huna bar Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Yitzḥak in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan: one who erred and skipped minḥa prays twice in the evening, and there is no 'its day passed, its offering is void'.

lines.speaker: Objection
lines.text: 'That which is crooked cannot be made straight' (Ecclesiastes 1:15) — this is one who omitted the evening or morning Shema or prayer. 'That which is wanting cannot be numbered' — one whose friends were counted for a mitzva and he was not among them.

lines.speaker: Resolution
lines.text: Rabbi Yitzḥak in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan: that baraita is about one who omitted deliberately (בְּמֵזִיד). Rav Ashi: the wording proves it — it says 'omitted' (בִּטֵּל), not 'erred' (טָעָה).

callout.label: Bottom line:
callout.text: An accidental omission is repaired by doubling the next Amida; a deliberate one is 'crooked' and cannot be straightened.

slides.title: 🕯️ Making Up Minḥa on Shabbat and the Havdala Puzzle
slides.subtitle: The baraita's rule and the Tosefta that contradicts it

steps.content: 1️⃣ Missed minḥa on Friday afternoon: pray two Amidas on Shabbat night
2️⃣ Missed minḥa on Shabbat: pray two weekday Amidas on Saturday night
3️⃣ Say havdala (in 'Who graciously grants knowledge') in the first, the real evening prayer — not in the second, which stands in for minḥa
4️⃣ If he said havdala in the second but not the first: the second counts, the first does not
5️⃣ So omitting havdala is like not praying at all, and he must repeat?

6️⃣ But the Tosefta: one who forgot 'the might of the rains' or the request for rain must repeat; one who forgot havdala in 'Who grants knowledge' does not, since he can say it over the cup. קַשְׁיָא — the contradiction stands

callout.label: Rabbi Yehuda's 'until':
callout.text: Does 'until four hours' include the fourth hour or not? The Gemara begins to answer from 'until pelag haminḥa': if 'until' excludes, Rabbi Yehuda differs from the Rabbis; if it includes… the answer continues on the next daf.

slides.title: 👴 Who Instituted the Three Daily Prayers?
slides.subtitle: Both views have a baraita behind them — and they end up reconciled

boxes.title: R' Yosei son of R' Ḥanina: the Patriarchs
items: Abraham — Shaḥarit: 'Abraham rose early in the morning to the place where he had stood' (Genesis 19:27); standing means prayer, as 'Pinehas stood up and prayed' (Psalms 106:30)

Isaac — Minḥa: 'Isaac went out to converse (לָשׂוּחַ) in the field toward evening' (Genesis 24:63); conversing means prayer, as 'a prayer of the afflicted… pours out his complaint (שִׂיחוֹ)' (Psalms 102:1)
Jacob — Ma'ariv: 'He encountered (וַיִּפְגַּע) the place and slept there' (Genesis 28:11); encountering means prayer, as 'do not encounter Me' (Jeremiah 7:16)

boxes.title: R' Yehoshua ben Levi: the daily offerings
items: The prayers parallel the tamid offerings in time and character
Shaḥarit until noon, or four hours — like the morning tamid
Minḥa until evening, or pelag — like the afternoon tamid
Ma'ariv unfixed — like the limbs and fats burning all night
Musaf all day, or seven hours — like the Musaf offering

boxes.title: Reconciliation
items: Is the offerings baraita a refutation of Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina?
He can answer: the Patriarchs instituted the prayers, and the Sages based them on the offerings (וְאַסְמְכִינְהוּ רַבָּנַן אַקׇּרְבָּנוֹת)
Proof: otherwise, who instituted Musaf according to him? No Patriarch did

callout.label: Why it matters:
callout.text: The Gemara links this dispute to the mishna's deadlines: if prayer times mirror the offerings, then Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis are really arguing about when each tamid may be brought.

summary.principle: Prayer has its hours because it stands in place of the Temple offerings, yet it remains a plea for mercy — so an honest mistake can be made up at the next prayer, while a deliberate omission cannot be straightened.

flowSteps.content: 🚽 End of chapter three: four cubits from filth behind him, out of sight in front; an unused bathroom or a Persian toilet is different. A zav who saw keri immerses — Rabbi Yehuda exempts
🕰️ Chapter four's mishna: Shaḥarit until noon (R' Yehuda: four hours), Minḥa until evening (R' Yehuda: pelag), Ma'ariv unfixed, Musaf all day (R' Yehuda: seven hours)

columns.content: 🔁 Erred and skipped a prayer → pray the next one twice, even minḥa at ma'ariv; 'its day passed' does not apply. Deliberate omission → 'crooked cannot be made straight'
🕯️ On Saturday night, havdala goes in the first Amida; the Tosefta's 'no need to repeat for havdala' leaves a kashya

flowSteps.content: 👴 Patriarchs instituted the prayers (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob), and the Sages anchored their times in the tamid offerings — which is why Musaf exists at all
🎓 Key Principle: Praying within the time earns the reward of 'prayer at its time'; praying late still earns the reward of prayer

quiz.q: According to Rav Huna, when is four cubits sufficient distance from feces for reciting Shema?
o: Only when the feces are in a Persian bathroom
When the feces are behind him; if in front, he must move until they are out of sight
When the feces are dry as earthenware
Only for Shema but not for prayer
quiz.e: Rava in the name of Rav Seḥora in the name of Rav Huna limits the mishna's four cubits to feces behind him; in front he distances himself as far as he can see, and the same applies to prayer.

quiz.q: Why does the Gemara say Rav Ḥisda permitted standing opposite a bathroom and praying?
o: Because it was a newly built bathroom that had never been used
Because the bathroom had a door
Because he held that designation as a bathroom has no effect
Because prayer is more lenient than Shema
quiz.e: After Rav Yosef bar Ḥanina's statement that even an empty bathroom counts as a bathroom, the Gemara explains Rav Ḥisda's case as a new structure built for the purpose but not yet used.

quiz.q: What reward does one receive for praying the morning prayer after noon?
o: No reward, since the time has passed
The full reward of prayer at its appointed time
The reward of prayer, but not the reward of prayer at its appointed time
Reward only if he prays twice
quiz.e: The Gemara reconciles the mishna with Rabbi Yoḥanan: one may pray all day, but only until noon does he receive the reward of prayer in its time; afterward he receives the reward of prayer alone.

quiz.q: How does the Gemara reconcile Rabbi Yoḥanan's allowance to make up a missed prayer with the baraita that 'that which is crooked cannot be made straight' refers to one who omitted a prayer?
o: The baraita refers only to the evening Shema
The baraita refers to one who omitted the prayer deliberately, whereas one who erred may make it up
The baraita follows Rabbi Yehuda, who is not the halakha
The baraita refers to a missed Musaf
quiz.e: Rabbi Yitzḥak in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan limits the baraita to deliberate omission, and Rav Ashi notes the precise wording: it says 'omitted', not 'erred'.

quiz.q: How does Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina answer the baraita that derives the prayer deadlines from the daily offerings?
o: He retracts and agrees the offerings instituted the prayers
The Patriarchs instituted the prayers, and the Sages later based their times on the offerings — otherwise who instituted Musaf?
The baraita follows Rabbi Yehuda alone
The offerings were themselves instituted by the Patriarchs
quiz.e: He maintains that Abraham, Isaac and Jacob instituted the three prayers while the Sages anchored them in the offerings. The proof is Musaf, which no Patriarch instituted and must therefore stem from the offerings.
